title: How money really moves in Towneers: a player's guide to the economy
html:
Every game with a currency teaches you the same lesson sooner or later: money you earn is only half the story, and the other half is where it leaves. In Towneers, a free multiplayer pixel-art city that runs in your browser, that second half is unusually visible. Rent comes due every game day, a café pays for electricity in every hour it is open, and the city itself buys your goods at a deliberately low price so that people have a reason to deal with each other. This guide is for players, not developers. It explains where gold comes from, where it goes, how prices work and what to do with that knowledge. Numbers come from the game's current settings, and the game is in alpha, so they can change.

▶ Play Towneers free in your browser

The two currencies

Gold 🪙 is the main money, all earned in the game; you start with 🪙600. Gems 💎 are optional and bought with real money. Everything in this guide works with gold alone.

One more unit matters: the game day. One game minute is one real second, so a game day lasts 24 real minutes. Rent and many fees are quoted per game day, which means bills arrive quickly if you are careless.

Where gold comes from

Think of income in three layers.

Layer one: gifts from the game

  • The tutorial hands you gold, 10 💎 and your own apartment.
  • The daily reward is a 7-day calendar; day 7 includes 🪙180, and every full week in a row adds 10% to the money, up to 50%.
  • Weekly goals arrive every Monday. Five goals each pay gold and experience, and finishing all five opens a chest with 🪙300 and 10 💎.
  • The Hall of Fame pays the top three of every weekly board 🪙500, 🪙250 and 🪙100.

Layer two: work paid by the city

The city offers 19 ways to earn. Couriers and street cleaners start at level 1 with no tools; fishers need only a rod; taxi drivers start at level 3 with their own car. Shifts in other people's places pay for the minutes you spend at your post, plus 🪙2 per customer and tips. Crafts such as cooking, carpentry, tailoring and mechanics turn raw items into goods worth more than their parts.

Layer three: money from other players

This is where the economy gets interesting. Players pay for quality goods, rare fish, three-star crops, furniture and shift work. A café owner posts a buy order, a stranger buys your lot overnight, a team pays you a share of a factory's profit. This money moves from one player's pocket to another's.

Where gold goes

Now the other direction. The recurring costs are the ones that surprise newcomers.

  • Rent. Apartments rent for 🪙44–78 per game day and houses for 🪙133–272. No rent is charged below level 5 or in your first 3 days. Owning removes the daily cost.
  • Business costs. A vacant premises rents for 🪙242–352 per game day, with up to 2 rented at once. On top come utilities for the hours you are open, supplies and wages.
  • Factory costs. A team's Workshop hall rents for 🪙150 per game day, the bigger Factory hall for 🪙350, and electricity is 🪙0.5 per kW per game hour.
  • Fees. The Trading House takes 5% of a sale from the seller. Buying from your phone adds a delivery charge to your Pickup cell, 5% with a minimum of 🪙2. Selling a house or a business to another player costs you 5%.
  • One-off purchases. A driving licence is 🪙150, a kick scooter 🪙220, a city bike 🪙680, a car from 🪙4,800 to 🪙42,000, a garage 🪙3,500, a stone plaque 🪙300, a team 🪙1,000.
  • Small daily spending. A bus ride is 🪙2, a taxi starts at 🪙5 and funfair tickets run 🪙3–15.

The healthy way to see it: a rented apartment or a rented premises is a subscription you are paying every 24 minutes of real time. Make sure the thing it enables earns more than it costs.

City floor versus player prices

The central rule of the economy is simple. The city covers the basics and buys from players at a floor, a little cheaper than players usually pay each other. Quality goods, rare fish, ★★★ crops and crafted furniture are worth selling to people.

The floor is not a trap; it is a safety net. You can always sell to the city instantly, so nothing in your bag is ever worthless. But the city lowers the price with each sale to the same shop, and for uncommon, rare and epic items it pays only a fraction of what players pay. It does not buy legendary items or dishes at all. A beginner guide from the game puts the usual city price at about 35% of retail.

Concrete examples

Fish. A perch has a base worth of 🪙16, a tuna 🪙90 and the legendary golden fish 🪙600. Kitchens pay a share of that worth, and the more you sell to the city in a day, the less each fish brings. In the game's illustrative story, a café owner posts a buy order for perch at 🪙20 each, up to 10 a day. The order's price does not drop with volume and does not count toward the city daily limit, so selling into it keeps the price steady however many fish you bring.

Crops. Pumpkins pay the most per piece: the city price is 🪙5.5 per star, and the farm co-op takes up to 20 a day per farmer at full price. The next 20 fall to 40%, the following 20 to 25%, then it stops until the next game day. Stars matter: the city pays ×1.15 for ★★ and ×1.3 for ★★★, and café orders, which ask for stars, pay more again.

Furniture. In the team factory guide, a chair costs about 🪙3 in materials against a wholesale price of 🪙19. That gap is why people build production chains.

Property. The city pays 70% of the value when you sell land, a building or a business back. A player pays what you agree.

Reading the Trading House

The Trading House is the player marketplace. Here is how to read it.

Lots. You list an item at your own price. Each player can have up to 12 listings, each lasting 7 days. The buyer pays exactly the listed price; you pay a 5% fee. A lot listed at 🪙100 therefore leaves you 🪙95. Unsold items wait in Pickup.

Players pay ≈. Each item card shows what players really pay, the median of deals over the last 7 days, once there are at least 5 deals between at least 4 players. Until then you see a guide based on the retail price. There is also a two-week price chart.

The Wanted tab. The 🔥 Wanted tab shows what people are looking for and at what price. If your bag holds something on that list, you can often sell it with one tap.

Trading with players opens at level 3, or one day after you create your character.

Check the chart before you sell anything.

Buy orders, from both sides

A buy order says: I will buy this many of this item at this price.

As a buyer

In the Trading House the money is reserved the moment you post the order, so sellers do not need to trust you. A venue owner posts orders under Manage, Storage, Buying from players, with the item, the price, how many per day and an optional daily budget. Each item has a price cap, higher for ★★, ★★★ and rare goods. The venue's cash register pays, and the goods go into its storage.

As a seller

An owner who bids too high drains their own till, because the same register pays utilities, rent and wages. That is why owners cap their orders.

Sell at the till with 💵 Sell, or sell into a Trading House order with one tap. The sheet tells you what will be taken. An owner's order does not lower its price as you sell and does not count against your daily limit with the city, so check orders before you take fish to a kitchen.

What a café really costs to run

A café is the classic first business, and its cost structure is a good lesson in every sink above.

Setup. One day of rent from 🪙242 plus café equipment of about 🪙2,810. An empty hall needs only the rent, and you add equipment as you earn.

Daily costs. Rent each game day, utilities for the opening hours, supplies and wages. A resident works an 8-hour shift, so a long day needs two shifts.

The first two days. For the first 48 game hours the city waives utilities and pays half of the residents' wages. Use the window to hire and tune the menu.

Pricing. At the recommended price, 9 guests in 10 buy. At double the price, only about a third do. Do the sum for ten guests: nine sales at the recommended price against about three at double. Unless your costs per sale are very high, the recommended price wins.

Where the money lives. Takings go to the till. From the till you pay costs and withdraw profit. You can also sell the café to the city for 70% of its value or to another player.

Growth. Business levels run from 1 to 10, rise with every sale and every guest, and each level brings more customers. A reputation for good shifts and a signature product help too.

Team payouts

A team factory is the most complex money flow in the game, but its rules are clear.

Cash box. The factory has a cash box. It receives money for deliveries to the city and for goods taken from the warehouse, and it pays rent, electricity, the shift master's wage (🪙14 per game hour) and construction purchases. If the cash box stays empty for three days in a row, the hall returns to the city.

Shares. Everything you put in earns permanent shares: gold counts one to one, a machine as an item counts at 40% of its catalogue price, materials at wholesale price, and one installation point counts as 🪙15. Shares stay with you if you leave, and the team can buy them out at book value.

Activity. Weekly work, such as installing, tuning recipes and adding raw materials, earns activity points. Someone who has not logged in for a while is paid by shares only.

The rule. The owner picks an amount above the reserve and a rule: 50/50 between shares and activity (the default), 70/30, 30/70 or all by shares. A payout over 🪙10,000 waits for a second signature from the Manager, and the 📜 Log shows who put in, took out and was paid. A Manager can withdraw up to 🪙2,000 per game day.

A running example. The bread chain runs on 11 kW. At 🪙0.5 per kW per game hour that is 🪙5.5 an hour, or 🪙132 over a full game day. A hired shift master keeps the factory going for up to 12 game hours at 🪙14 an hour, which is 🪙168. Add the hall's rent of 🪙150 per game day and you can see roughly what the chain must earn before anyone is paid.

Ten practical money rules

  1. Take every gift. Daily reward, weekly goals and the tutorial are free. Streaks multiply the daily reward.
  2. Check the price before you sell. Open the item card, read Players pay ≈ and the chart.
  3. Do not dump on the city. Each sale to the same shop lowers the next price. Spread sales or find a player.
  4. Look at buy orders first. An owner's order does not drop with volume.
  5. Sell quality, not quantity. ★★ and ★★★ earn a premium from the city and more from players.
  6. Diversify crops. The co-op quota is per crop and per farmer, so three crops beat one.
  7. Never rent more than you earn. Rent is due every 24 real minutes.
  8. Keep a reserve. A team cash box with an empty reserve can lose its hall.
  9. Price at the recommended level. Doubling a price loses most buyers.
  10. Build relationships. Reputation, a good shift and a regular customer are worth more than two extra coins per fish.

Questions and answers

Do I need to spend real money to earn gold?

No. All gold is earned in the game, and every job, business, home and farm works with it. Gems 💎 and Premium are optional.

Why does the city pay less than players?

By design. The city covers the basics and buys at a floor so that quality goods are worth selling to people.

What is the safest early income?

Courier work from level 1, the daily reward and the weekly goals. Fishing needs only a rod, and kitchens buy your catch.

How do I know a fair price?

Open the item card. It shows what players usually pay and a two-week chart. If there are too few deals, you see a guide based on retail.

Does a lot ever disappear?

A lot lasts 7 days. If it does not sell, the item waits in Pickup.

Can I get rich without a business?

Yes. Farmers, fishers, crafters and shift workers earn steadily, and top positions on weekly boards pay 🪙500, 🪙250 and 🪙100.

What is the cheapest way to get a home?

Rent an apartment from 🪙44 a day, free below level 5. The cheapest land is a farm plot from 🪙2,700.

Can I sell property?

Yes. The city pays 70% of the value, and a player pays what you agree, minus the city's 5%.

Is the economy final?

No. The game is in alpha, so balance and prices can change, and the world may be reset.

Where to start

Open the game, finish the tutorial, take the reward and pick one income source. Then look at the Trading House and notice what other people want. Once you can read prices, the rest of the economy follows.
